Met boat from our marina on the way back.
These bastards found us on the middle of the galveston bay, hundreds of them!!! They do not bite, donot sting, but annoying too much!
At the 3pm wind completely died below 2 kn and we started engine and motored last hour of the trip back.
Story first.
I have a NOCO GEN5X3 three-bank charger on board for my Start, House, and Windlass batteries.
It worked quite well for about five years, keeping my lead-acid batteries topped up. Then I switched the House battery to LiFePO₄ and changed that charger bank to Lithium mode.
At first, everything looked good.

I also have a 40A, 14.2V power supply that runs the boat's 12V system from shore power while I'm connected at the marina. The battery and power supply were combined through a 100A ideal-diode module. It works similarly to ordinary diodes, but with a very small voltage drop.
One night while I was sleeping on the boat, I noticed the lights periodically blinking and my main navigation computer restarting every 10–15 seconds.
At first, it was a mystery.

I checked for a heavy load, loose connections, bad wiring, or anything else that might cause the voltage to collapse. Eventually, I noticed that the NOCO charger was showing an "Overvoltage" error on the LiFePO₄ battery.
That was surprising.
I checked the battery BMS, and it showed nothing suspicious—the battery was simply at 100% state of charge.

Then I discovered that the battery BMS was a little too smart. When the battery reaches 100% SOC, the BMS simply disconnects the charging path. It doesn't report a fault; it just puts the battery into a discharge-only state.
This created an interesting problem.

The battery was fully charged, but after resting its terminal voltage dropped back to approximately 13.9–14.0V. The charger saw this voltage and eventually decided that it should charge the battery again.
But the battery was already full, and the BMS had disabled charging.
So when the charger attempted to start charging, the current had nowhere useful to go and produced a short voltage spike of approximately 16.5V.
The battery could not absorb the spike, so it propagated toward the ideal-diode module.

The module detected that the battery-side voltage had suddenly become higher and quickly switched the source selection. Because the pulse was very short, this confused the ideal-diode power-sharing arrangement and produced both a voltage spike and a following voltage dip on the 12V house bus.
My computer's protection socket detected the abnormal voltage and shut the computer down to protect it.
A few seconds later everything recovered—and then the entire sequence happened again.
That experience pushed me to design my own smart power switch like UPS.
The new system has several important features:
Shore power has priority.
If the power-supply output is above approximately 12V, the 12V house bus is powered from the PSU regardless of battery voltage.
Complete source isolation.
Each source uses a dual-MOSFET switch arranged so that, when OFF, current cannot flow through the switch in either direction. This completely isolates the battery and power supply from each other.
Minimum battery run time.

If the system switches to the battery because the PSU voltage falls too low, it remains on battery power for at least 10 seconds. This prevents rapid back-and-forth switching if shore-power voltage is unstable.
Break-before-make switching.
There is approximately a 100 µs dead time between disconnecting one source and connecting the other, ensuring that the battery and PSU are never directly connected together during a transition.
What started as a strange blinking-light problem turned into a complete engineering project:
Idea → Solution Research → Schematic Design → PCB Design → Component Sourcing → Assembly → Programming → Functional Testing → Stress Testing → 3D Enclosure Design → Installation → On-Board Testing
After about four weeks of work, everything is installed and working properly.

And now, instead of trusting two power sources and an ideal-diode module to negotiate with each other, I have a power-management system whose behavior I actually understand and keep things under control.
Board built and covered with conformal coating.
Module installed in the engine compartment.

title: Days#278 Galveston bay sailing with friends, cleaning lazarette

blocks.t: We had a great time out on the water this weekend. It was my birthday, and we spent six lovely hours on the bay.
The water was almost flat, and the wind was just 3–6 knots—perfect for a relaxing day. No sporty sailing, no drills, less than 10 degrees of heel, and speeds of 2–5.5 knots—whatever the wind gave us.
We even enjoyed hot tea and birthday cake (Napoleon) underway, thanks to our big boy: a 3.5 kWh battery and a 3 kW inverter
Just me
Next day little work on boat was done. But Coffee is the first.
So, what got done:
A little software fix before we headed out.

I fixed an annoyance with the NavPod: the button to activate the autopilot didn’t automatically set the current heading as the target heading. Now it works as autopilots normally do—press AUTO, and the boat continues on its current heading.
Adding a cockpit shower.

The work is partially done: the cold water line is routed to the lazarette, and a ball valve and shower head are connected to the pressurized water system. For now, the shower head and hose just sit in the lazarette. To use the shower, I need to open the hatch and pull them out.
Why only half done? Because I plan to add a thermostatic mixing valve and install a shower outlet in the cockpit. But that will come later.
Cleaning the lazarette. Boat yoga.
It hadn’t been cleaned since the repairs and had accumulated a lot of fiberglass dust and dirt.

sections.title: Reef blocks and winches installation design

blocks.t: As you remember I made 4 reefs on my new main sail, and 4-th i would likely never use ;)
I tried to calculate what could be loads in reef lines on my boat and get really surprised numbers.
My sail:
ConfigurationLuff remainingEstimated areaFull-sail area
Full sail11.14 m25.60 m²100%
At fourth reef set, about 4.9 m² of mainsail remains exposed to the wind.
At a worst-case wind speed of 60 knots, that sail area produces approximately 3.7 kN force.

If about 40% reaches the reef clew, the clew must take 1.5 kN. Because the two reef-line legs pull at a shallow angle of about 10°, each leg carries approximately (1.5 ÷ [2 × \sin(10°)] = 4.3) kN. Allowing a 50% increase for gusts, flogging and shock x1.5 = 6.4 kN. so, a reef block i need for about 8 kN working load.
The same logic calculation gives us about the same loads on all reefs.
ReefSail areaMaximum windTotal sail forceNormal line tensionPeak line tension
Reef 119.2 m²20 kn1.62 kN1.86 kN2.80 kN
Reef 213.6 m²30 kn2.58 kN2.97 kN4.45 kN
Reef 38.8 m²40 kn2.97 kN3.42 kN5.13 kN
Reef 44.9 m²60 kn3.72 kN4.29 kN6.43 kN
6kN if about 350lb, no way to pull it by hands, so I need to have winches to be able to set right tension.
BUT, with reasonable use winch must not exceed MWL for lines and construction.
so, I selected #10 winches with "reasonable high" cranking force person may do is 70lb with x10 advantage 700lb. So, we good here.
Next challenge - curvature of the boom. I would need curvature following spacers to install the blocks and winches.

So far I am looking to use 3D printed ASA plastic with 100% infill to make them. 3D-printed ASA spacers is what I can match the boom’s curvature instead of trying to force a flat block onto a curved surface. With 100% infill and about 2,400 mm² of support area, even approximately 12 kN of total screw-clamping force creates only around 5 MPa of average pressure. ASA can comfortably support this.

From inside, washers would concentrate the load around four small spots risk of make dents local cracking. The full size backing plate ties all four M5 screws together and spreads the pulling and twisting forces across the complete mounting area.
Plastic also has some plasticity and able to form better connection between spacer and boom surface.

I install blocks and winches to the mast using 3D printed spacers to follow boom curvature and distribute load. ASA plastic calculated like good enough material for this. Back side is I will need to make sure i will retight screws several times after installation.

One side of the spacer is flat, other following boom surface. Also spacer is asimetrical to install one block 10mm higher than boom equator and other 10mm lower to let reef lines closer to boom end go freely without touching other reef block.
from inside the boob another spacer installed to align backing plate be in parallel with the block.
Backing plates are 3mm SS304 flat steel with tapered holes. center hole is to put screw to keep plate on the spacer.
Backing plates are 5mm SS. small screws keep plate at place.
In dreams all looks well ontill some stuburn screw appeared to stuck.
I think engineers who use slotted round-head screws in places where they can seize have a special place in hell.
Disassembling was relatively simple with help of impact screwdriver, BUT one from 20 screws made me more problems than all other together!
After several times screw bit jumped out of screw and scratchcard my hands I realized why you will not find slot screwdriver bits for impact screwdriver. They just jump out and injury your hands.
What i did - I put a nut with hole a size of screw head diameter. and tie it to boom with duct tape!
then easy undo this screw without any risk on screwdriver jump out of slot.
Bastard in hands.
Reason why i stripped it is simple - I need to put backing plates inside the boom and screws sticking inside are not helping any.
Put external spacer and use it as template to drill holes
Use hot glue gun to glue backing plate to wood slat, then route tiny steel rope th
Then use this steel ripe to pull backing plate to close enough to align screw holes and put screws.
When holes aligned - drill a small hole (only in aluminum) on the center, countersink it and put small screw to keep backing block on place.
Apply tefgel on the screw and aluminum holes and install the block! is it look nice?
Backing plates, same approach.
Dryfit before put the winch, then winch at place
Starboard side Reef1 and Reef3 (reef1 block I left original)
Port side Reef2 and Reef4 blocks, outhaul line on the top.
Winch and cleat for reefs on the each side on the boom.

It is very interesting, there a lot of double braid anchor ropes, but how people splice them to chains to let it go thru the windlass. just doing eye splice is not working connecting point appears too big and too stiff to go thru gypsy. My solution is to upbraid core and cover (keep plaints intact) and re-braid plaints it in 8 plaints rope ( core is 8 plaints originally). Then do 8 plaints rope to chain splicing.
Probably it is temporary solution, but look not so bad.

title: Day#280, Refrigerator thermostat,  WattCycle batteries monitor, Bumpy sailing

blocks.t: This project started four years ago. I used components from a household refrigerator to convert my icebox into a powered refrigerator. After four years, I had to replace the compressor with a 12V DC model, which I had planned to do from the beginning. So far, everything has worked well with an inexpensive Chinese-made thermostat like this one.
Link to AliExpress

However, I went through three of these thermostats in four years. I think the main problem lies in the sensor and sensing circuit: moisture and vibration seem to make them unreliable. After just a few days, the latest one started showing +26°C when the refrigerator was cold and +2°C when the box was warm. Maybe interference from the AC power lines affected it, but I got tired of fighting this battle.

Welcome to my life ;-) I decided to design my own solution with a 1-Wire digital temperature sensor, remote refrigerator control, a connection to my boat computer, a food safety alarm if the temperature stays above 7°C for too long, and additional compressor protection.
I built the thermostat around an ESP-12F module, which is a great fit for this kind of project.
Board designed for small IP68 project box.
Full user manuals are here
Schematic/BOM/Gerbers on request
What basic functions.
Control temperature in the box.
Control fan inside the box if you have one.
May control variable speed DC compressor to to boost cool when needed.
With additional sensors _may_ monitor freezer volume temperature, compressor, condenser, evaporator temperatures and notify you with errors.
all errors may be disabled if if not needed.
Main interface is simple as it could be - one button, one RGB LED in the button, buzzer.
It provides simple on/off function, mute alarms and check alarm codes when problem happen.
Indicator shows current state, but likely all of time it will be just blue ;)
2 light modes day and night (to dim indicator and do not blind you at night
Advanced interface (Web interface over WIFI)
Here you can do everything
Set temperature
Assign temperature sensors to functions if you use more than one.
Set alarm temperatures
Enable/disable alarms.
MINOR - keeps cooling (red flash every 5 s)
11 Door open - close the door
22 Cooler below 0 °C - check set temperature
24 Freezer below -25 °C - check the freezer
25 Extra sensor lost - check its wiring
26 Cooler above 10 °C - check door and load
27 Freezer above -5 °C - check door and load
31 Compressor hot - check ventilation
32 Condenser too hot - check fan and airflow
35 Evaporator below -30 °C - check for ice
FOOD SAFETY - keeps cooling (amber LED)
21 Cooler warm 30 min - check food, double-click
23 Freezer warm 30 min - check food, double-click
MAJOR - cooling stopped (steady red LED)
51 Not cooling - service needed, then power cycle
52 Cooler sensor lost - check sensor, power cycle
53 Compressor overheated - cool down, power cycle
Compressor related settings
Firmware update over web interface
Web interface has two modes BASIC and ADVANCED
MQTT - connection can be used to integrate thermostat to your OpenPlotter infrastructure
Serial port - for "nice" display, but i think it is overkill
Web interface screen examples
Designed WattCycle batteries monitor talking to batteries over BT and show current battery state.
Also sends data to SignalK server (openplotter)

title: Updated 11/9/26 - Refrigerator lid.

blocks.t: Originally, refrigerator lid had zero insulation inside, it was just plug to close hole in the countertop.
When I switch to refrigerator i want better insulation as well I want to be able to close lid air tight to eliminate excessive ice build on evaporator coil due to humid air condensation.
For 4 years it was gust piece of isolation foam. Now is the time to make real lid.
I 3d modeled 2 parts:
external frame - it will be glued in the refrigerator opening and sealed around insulation then epoxied to the walls to prevent refrigerator top insulation to get wet.
Internal insert - similar shape but nested inside frame intended to be the shell for the lid. It will be filled with foam.and glassed over to protect foam from absorbing water.
In between the frame, and lid will be gasket
Printing the parts. Parts printed with 0.8mm thickness. They are just king of shape making core to glass them over.
This is refrigerator top opening I need to close.
External frame dry fit. Frame must be little cut to size on place (boat is far from to be square and parallel)
Lid shell bottom and internal side of the walls was glassed with one layer of CSM.
External frame glassed from outside. (it is sitting over the lid)
In between boat days I maintained frame and lid with topside paint (just to make it white and seal 3D printed parts.
Ready for sealing edges...
Sealed refrigerator foam insulation with epoxy and installed the frame.
Lid is assembled.

blocks.t: After 4 years I decided to replace windlass motor with brand new one.

My motor sometimes dropping power during long hard run. I know the problem, when i repaired it i could not find right brush springs and installed what I had in hands. Very likely one of springs is loosing strength when brush at getting hot. I plan to replace springs and keep old motor as as spare.
During that work Vic found the both shackles on the anchor chain are cracked, When I have undone pins i was able to break them in half by hands. I can't imagine how i did not lost my anchor!!!!!
Replaced with Zinc galvanized. Really no sense to have stainless shackles in between galvanized anchor and galvanized chain.
Finished build a lid. Refrigerator project officially complete.
